name: James Clark
milestone_by_age_26: Released groff 0.3.1 in June 1990, the first version of his from-scratch GNU implementation of the Unix troff typesetting system, which became a standard part of Linux.
early_history_summary: Educated at Charterhouse School and Merton College, Oxford (Mathematics and Philosophy, Class I Honours), Clark began writing open source software around 1987. He started work on groff in early 1989 as a contribution to the GNU Project, motivated by an interest in typography from reading the TeXBook and the lack of a free troff implementation.
family_context_summary: Born into the Sainsbury family, one of the UK's wealthiest retail dynasties; maternal grandfather Robert Sainsbury was a major art collector and philanthropist, maternal uncle David Sainsbury (Baron Sainsbury of Turville) was a businessman and politician.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of parental domain expertise in computing or software; family wealth came from the Sainsbury retail empire on the maternal side.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite education, family wealth, GNU open source community, Sainsbury family
evidence_summary: Clark's path to groff was enabled by an elite education at Charterhouse and Oxford, funded by his connection to the Sainsbury family. He taught himself typesetting and C++ programming, writing groff from scratch before C++ was standardized. The GNU Project provided a community and distribution channel for his work. No evidence of parental tech domain expertise or dedicated mentorship was found in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born into the Sainsbury family (UK retail dynasty) in London; maternal grandfather Robert Sainsbury was a major art collector, maternal uncle David Sainsbury (Baron Sainsbury). Educated at Charterhouse School and Merton College, Oxford.
current_position: Lives in Bangkok, Thailand as a permanent resident; owns Thai Open Source Software Center; continues open-source work including the Ballerina programming language at WSO2.

trajectory.event: Released groff 0.3.1, the first version of his GNU implementation of troff, which became a standard part of Linux.
Released groff 1.04, the first stable version; began work on SGML with the sgmls parser.
Moved to Bangkok, Thailand and established the Thai Open Source Software Center.
Served as technical lead for the W3C XML working group that developed the XML 1.0 Recommendation.
Awarded the first XML Cup for contributions to XML development.
Co-authored the RELAX NG specification, a schema language for XML.
Co-created the Ballerina programming language at WSO2.

name: Dave Winer
milestone_by_age_26: Founded Living Videotext in 1983 at age 28; first product ThinkTank shipped in 1983. By age 26, was developing outliner software independently after leaving Personal Software, but had not yet founded a company or shipped a product.

name: Adam Curry
milestone_by_age_26: Became a VJ for MTV in 1987 at age 23, hosting Headbangers Ball and MTV Top 20 Video Countdown, interviewing stars like Michael Jackson and Paul McCartney.
early_history_summary: Born in Arlington, Virginia, Curry moved to the Netherlands at age 8 and began working in Dutch pirate radio as a teenager under the pseudonym 'John Holden.' He rose to host the Dutch weekly pop-music TV program Countdown and other shows for broadcast station Veronica before being recruited by MTV in 1987.
family_context_summary: Described as coming from a 'communications/government family'; specific details about parents' professions not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: pirate radio, Dutch broadcasting, early specialization, MTV, cable TV wave
evidence_summary: Curry built his broadcasting career through early, hands-on repetition: starting in Dutch pirate radio as a teenager, he progressed to hosting national TV and radio shows in the Netherlands before landing an MTV VJ role at 23. His family was described as being in 'communications/government,' suggesting some domain proximity. The cable TV explosion of the 1980s provided a structural wave that amplified his reach. No evidence of significant financial privilege or dedicated mentorship was found.
starting_point: Born in Arlington, Virginia to a communications/government family; grew up in Amstelveen, Netherlands from age 8, working in pirate radio as a teenager.
current_position: Co-hosts the No Agenda podcast with John C. Dvorak; co-founded Podcast Index; resides in the US; earned substantial wealth from sale of OnRamp/Think New Ideas during the dot-com era.

trajectory.event: Became a VJ for MTV, hosting Headbangers Ball and MTV Top 20 Video Countdown.
Registered mtv.com, one of the first celebrity-managed domain names, launching his internet career.
Co-founded Think New Ideas Inc., which IPO'd on NASDAQ during the dot-com bubble.
Co-founded PodShow (later Mevio), helping pioneer the podcasting medium.
Launched the No Agenda podcast with John C. Dvorak, which became a long-running independent podcast.
Co-founded Podcast Index, a decentralized podcast directory preserving open RSS-based podcasting.

name: Ben Goodger
milestone_by_age_26: Served as lead engineer for Firefox 1.0, released in November 2004 at age 24, which challenged Microsoft's Internet Explorer dominance and grew to tens of millions of users.
early_history_summary: Born in London and raised in Auckland, New Zealand, Goodger grew up without home internet access due to cost. He began building websites at around age 17 using his mother's workplace computer. As a second-year computer engineering student at the University of Auckland, he discovered the Mozilla Project and began contributing code. His work was noticed by Netscape engineers, who offered him a job at age 19; he interned at Netscape in 2000 and took on a larger role in the Firefox project.
family_context_summary: Raised by his mother, an accountant, in Auckland, New Zealand; family could not afford home internet access. Goodger would use his mother's workplace computer to upload websites he built at home.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother was an accountant; no evidence of family domain expertise in technology or software.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Mozilla open source, self-taught, financial constraint, Netscape internship, Firefox team
evidence_summary: Goodger's path to Firefox lead engineer was driven by self-taught web development and volunteer contributions to the Mozilla open-source community, which he discovered as a university student in Auckland. His family's limited finances meant no home internet, creating urgency to seek access at university and his mother's workplace. Netscape engineer David Hyatt noticed his contributions and recommended him for a job at 19. The open-source browser movement provided both a learning platform and a distribution channel for his work.
starting_point: Born in London, grew up in Auckland, New Zealand with his mother, an accountant; family could not afford home internet access.
current_position: VP at OpenAI leading the Atlas browser project; previously VP at Google leading Chrome UX; lives in San Francisco.

trajectory.event: Began contributing to the Mozilla open-source project as a computer engineering student at the University of Auckland.
Hired as an intern at Netscape in Mountain View after his Mozilla contributions were noticed by engineer David Hyatt.
Led engineering for Firefox 1.0, the open-source browser that challenged Microsoft's Internet Explorer dominance.
Joined Google to lead user experience for the Chrome browser project.
Joined OpenAI to lead development of the Atlas browser, aiming to challenge Chrome.

name: Sundar Pichai
milestone_by_age_26: Joined Google in 2004 at age 32; by age 26, held an MS from Stanford and was working as a product manager at Applied Materials. No material milestone by 26 found.

name: Marissa Mayer
milestone_by_age_26: Joined Google in 1999 as employee #20 and its first woman software engineer at age 24, developing and designing Google's search offerings during the company's critical early growth period.
early_history_summary: Born in Wausau, Wisconsin, Mayer excelled in academics and extracurriculars at Wausau West High School, including debate team captain and pom-pom squad captain. She attended Stanford University, earning a BS in Symbolic Systems and an MS in Computer Science with a specialization in AI. During her studies, she worked at SRI International and the UBS research lab in Zurich. After graduating, she received 14 job offers and joined Google in 1999.
family_context_summary: Daughter of Margaret Mayer, an art teacher of Finnish descent, and Michael Mayer, an environmental engineer who worked for water companies. Middle-class family in Wausau, Wisconsin. Grandfather Clem Mayer served as mayor of Jackson, Wisconsin for 32 years.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an environmental engineer and mother an art teacher; no direct family domain expertise in computer science or tech, though father's engineering background provided some STEM proximity.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Stanford, Silicon Valley, Google early team, Symbolic Systems, search wave
evidence_summary: Mayer's path to Google employee #20 was enabled by Stanford's elite CS program and its Silicon Valley location, which positioned her at the epicenter of the internet search wave. Her middle-class Wisconsin background provided no special financial platform or inherited tech network. Stanford's Symbolic Systems program and her AI research experience gave her the credentials that Google's founders valued. The explosive growth of Google's search product provided the structural wave that amplified her early contributions.
starting_point: Born in Wausau, Wisconsin to an environmental engineer father and art teacher mother; middle-class family; excelled in academics and extracurriculars at Wausau West High School.
current_position: Co-founder and CEO of Sunshine, a tech startup focused on AI-powered contact management; estimated net worth ~$540M; resides in the San Francisco Bay Area.

trajectory.event: Joined Google as employee #20 and its first woman software engineer, developing and designing Google's search offerings.
Promoted to VP of Search Products and User Experience at Google, overseeing products including Gmail and Google Maps.
Became CEO and President of Yahoo!, tasked with turning around the struggling internet portal.
Departed Yahoo! after its sale to Verizon for $4.8 billion.
Co-founded Sunshine, a startup focused on AI-powered contact management.

name: Sheryl Sandberg
milestone_by_age_26: By age 26, had earned an MBA from Harvard (1995) and was working at McKinsey; her material milestones (Treasury chief of staff at 27, Google VP at 32, Facebook COO at 39) all came after age 26.

name: Anne Wojcicki
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded 23andMe in 2006 at age 33; by age 26, was a healthcare research analyst at Investor AB on Wall Street. No material milestone by 26 found.

name: Eric Schmidt
milestone_by_age_26: Co-authored Lex, the standard Unix lexical analyzer generator, with Mike Lesk at Bell Labs in 1975 at age 20; Lex became a fundamental tool in compiler construction and remains widely used.
early_history_summary: Born in Falls Church, Virginia, Schmidt described himself as a 'hardcore programmer from age 14.' He graduated from Yorktown High School in 1972 and attended Princeton University, earning a BSE in electrical engineering in 1976. During summers at Bell Labs as an intern, he and Mike Lesk wrote Lex, with Schmidt designing, writing, and debugging the code. He later earned an MS (1979) and PhD (1982) in computer science from UC Berkeley.
family_context_summary: Born to Eleanor Schmidt, who held a master's degree in psychology, and Wilson Emerson Schmidt, a professor of international economics at Virginia Tech and Johns Hopkins who worked at the U.S. Treasury during the Nixon Administration. Schmidt spent part of his childhood in Italy due to his father's work.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an economics professor with government ties; no direct family domain expertise in computer science, but academic household provided intellectual environment and access to elite education.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Bell Labs, Princeton, Unix, Lex, Mike Lesk, early programming, academic family
evidence_summary: Schmidt's early milestone was catalyzed by access to Bell Labs as a Princeton undergraduate intern, placing him at the epicenter of Unix development in the 1970s. His professor father provided an academic household that valued intellectual achievement. Starting programming at 14, he had accumulated significant experience by the time he co-authored Lex at 20. Mike Lesk served as a collaborator and mentor at Bell Labs. The Unix wave at Bell Labs was the structural force that amplified his contributions.
starting_point: Born in Falls Church, Virginia; father was a professor of international economics at Virginia Tech and Johns Hopkins who worked at the U.S. Treasury; mother held a master's in psychology; spent part of childhood in Italy.
current_position: Co-founder of Schmidt Futures philanthropy; CEO of Relativity Space; estimated net worth ~$30 billion; resides in Atherton, California.

trajectory.event: Co-authored Lex with Mike Lesk at Bell Labs, creating the standard Unix lexical analyzer generator.
Joined Sun Microsystems as its first software manager, later rising to CTO.
Became CEO of Novell, a networking software company.
Became CEO of Google, guiding its transformation from startup to global tech giant.
Transitioned to Executive Chairman of Google (and later Alphabet), stepping down as CEO.
Founded Schmidt Futures, a philanthropic initiative investing in AI and scientific talent.
